newsitem.title: KENYA: Foreign UNHCR staff leave Eritrea, UNHCR source.
newsitem.headline: Foreign UNHCR staff leave Eritrea, UNHCR source.

text.p: Six foreign staff of the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR have left Eritrea, a UNHCR source said on Wednesday, after they were ordered out by the government apparently because of a row over Eritrean refugee status.
The source said five staff and their families left the Eritrean capital Asmara on Tuesday and flew to Nairobi. The head of mission, Arnulv Torbjornsen, later left on a flight to Geneva.
The source said one foreign staff member remained in Asmara on Wednesday. "We negotiated this person would leave at the end of the week as this staff member is an administrative officer," he added.
The source declined to say why the foreign staff had left.
But state television said last Friday the government had given UNHCR 48 hours to leave the country, saying without elaboration that it had circulated documents without authority.
Aid agency sources said later Eritrea had extended the period to 96 hours, giving UNHCR until midnight on Tuesday.
The UNHCR director of operations for central, east and west Africa, Albert-Alain Peters, visited Eritrea late last month and said Eritrea was dragging its feet on repatriation of Eritrean refugees.
He said he had raised with the government the possibility of UNHCR abandoning responsibility for Eritrean refugees, in official terms "cessation" of their refugee status.
UNHCR figures show some 145,000 Eritreans remain in refugee camps in Sudan, four years after the country became independent. In addition, there is an Eritrean urban population in Sudan.
Eritrea and Sudan broke diplomatic relations in December 1994, when Eritrea accused the Khartoum government of sending Moslem fundamentalist guerrillas across their common border.
Under the "cessation clause", all Eritreans holding refugee status anywhere in the world would lose that status and would no longer be able to approach any government as refugees.
Eritrea became independent in May 1993 after a 30-year guerrilla war against the government in Ethiopia.
